claim: Models of sound localization commonly assume that sound lateralization from interaural time differences is level invariant.
source: Models of sound localization commonly assume that sound lateralization from interaural time differences is level invariant.
evidence: This is a statement about existing models in the field, representing established knowledge about common assumptions in sound localization modeling.

claim: The labelled-line model encodes location through tuned representations of spatial location.
source: The labelled-line model encodes location through tuned representations of spatial location and predicts that perceived direction is level invariant.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the labelled-line model based on established theoretical frameworks in neuroscience.

claim: The labelled-line model predicts that perceived direction is level invariant.
source: The labelled-line model encodes location through tuned representations of spatial location and predicts that perceived direction is level invariant.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the properties of the labelled-line model.

claim: The hemispheric-difference model encodes location through spike-rate.
source: In contrast, the hemispheric-difference model encodes location through spike-rate and predicts that perceived direction becomes medially biased at low sound levels.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the hemispheric-difference model based on established theoretical frameworks.

claim: The hemispheric-difference model predicts that perceived direction becomes medially biased at low sound levels.
source: In contrast, the hemispheric-difference model encodes location through spike-rate and predicts that perceived direction becomes medially biased at low sound levels.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the properties of the hemispheric-difference model.

claim: Softer sounds are perceived closer to midline than louder sounds in human sound localization.
source: Here, behavioral experiments find that softer sounds are perceived closer to midline than louder sounds, favoring rate-coding models of human sound localization.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral experiments conducted in this study.

claim: The finding that softer sounds are perceived closer to midline favors rate-coding models of human sound localization.
source: Here, behavioral experiments find that softer sounds are perceived closer to midline than louder sounds, favoring rate-coding models of human sound localization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing experimental results with model predictions.

claim: Visual depth perception, which is based on interocular disparity, depends on the contrast of the target.
source: Analogously, visual depth perception, which is based on interocular disparity, depends on the contrast of the target.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in visual neuroscience.

claim: The brain may use a canonical computation of location that encodes perceived location through population spike rate relative to baseline.
source: The similar results in hearing and vision suggest that the brain may use a canonical computation of location: encoding perceived location through population spike rate relative to baseline.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the analogy between auditory and visual findings.

claim: Interaural time differences (ITDs) of the sounds reaching the ears allow listeners to localize sound in the horizontal plane.
source: For instance, interaural time differences (ITDs) of the sounds reaching the ears allow listeners to localize sound in the horizontal plane.
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory neuroscience.

claim: The medial superior olive (MSO) is the first neural processing stage where ITDs are encoded on the timescale of microseconds in the ascending mammalian auditory pathway.
source: In the ascending mammalian auditory pathway, the first neural processing stage where ITDs are encoded, on the timescale of microseconds, is the medial superior olive (MSO).
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory neuroscience.

claim: In the MSO, temporally precise binaural inputs converge, and their ITDs are converted to neural firing rate.
source: Here, temporally precise binaural inputs converge, and their ITDs are converted to neural firing rate (Goldberg and Brown, 1968; Yin and Chan, 1990; Spitzer and Semple, 1995; Pecka et al., 2010; Day and Semple, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: The shape of the MSO output firing rate curves as a function of ITD resembles that of a cross-correlation operation on the inputs to each ear.
source: The shape of the MSO output firing rate curves as a function of ITD resembles that of a cross-correlation operation on the inputs to each ear (Batra and Yin, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: The labelled-line model for sound localization was originally proposed by Jeffress (1948).
source: One prominent neural model for sound localization, originally proposed by Jeffress (1948), consists of a labelled line of coincidence detector neurons that are sensitive to the binaural synchronicity of neural inputs from each ear, with each neuron maximally sensitive to a specific magnitude of ITD (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a historical citation of the original proposal.

claim: The labelled-line model consists of a labelled line of coincidence detector neurons that are sensitive to the binaural synchronicity of neural inputs from each ear, with each neuron maximally sensitive to a specific magnitude of ITD.
source: One prominent neural model for sound localization, originally proposed by Jeffress (1948), consists of a labelled line of coincidence detector neurons that are sensitive to the binaural synchronicity of neural inputs from each ear, with each neuron maximally sensitive to a specific magnitude of ITD (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the structure of the labelled-line model with reference to a figure.

claim: The labelled-line model is computationally equivalent to a neural place-code based on bandlimited cross-correlations of the sounds reaching both ears.
source: This labelled-line model is computationally equivalent to a neural place-code based on bandlimited cross-correlations of the sounds reaching both ears (Domnitz and Colburn, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Several studies support the existence of labelled-line neural place-code mechanisms in the avian brain.
source: Several studies support the existence of labelled-line neural place-code mechanisms in the avian brain (Carr and Konishi, 1988; Overholt et al., 1992), and versions of it have successfully been applied in many engineering applications predicting human localization performance (e.g. Durlach, 1963; Hafter, 1971; Stern and Trahiotis, 1995; Breebaart et al., 2001; Hartmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Versions of the labelled-line model have successfully been applied in many engineering applications predicting human localization performance.
source: Several studies support the existence of labelled-line neural place-code mechanisms in the avian brain (Carr and Konishi, 1988; Overholt et al., 1992), and versions of it have successfully been applied in many engineering applications predicting human localization performance (e.g. Durlach, 1963; Hafter, 1971; Stern and Trahiotis, 1995; Breebaart et al., 2001; Hartmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Evidence from experiments on Mongolian gerbils shows that sharply tuned bilateral inhibitory inputs to the MSO play a crucial role in processing ITDs.
source: One reason for an alternative is that two excitatory inputs should suffice to implement the labelled-line model, but evidence from experiments on Mongolian gerbils shows that in addition to bilateral excitatory inputs, sharply tuned bilateral inhibitory inputs to the MSO play a crucial role in processing ITDs (Brand et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: To date no labelled-line type neurons encoding auditory space have been discovered in a mammalian species.
source: Moreover, to date no labelled-line type neurons encoding auditory space have been discovered in a mammalian species.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Several studies proposed that mammalian sound localization can be modeled based on differences in firing rates across the two populations of neurons that are tuned to opposing hemispheres.
source: Indeed, using a population rate-code, several studies proposed that mammalian sound localization can be modeled based on differences in firing rates across the two populations of neurons that are tuned to opposing hemispheres (Figure 1B; van Bergeijk, 1962; McAlpine and Grothe, 2003; Devore et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies and illustrated in a figure.

claim: Rate-based models generally predict that neuronal responses carry most information at the steepest slopes of neural-discharge-rate versus ITD curves.
source: Rate-based models generally predict that neuronal responses carry most information at the steepest slopes of neural-discharge-rate versus ITD curves, where neural discharge changes most strongly (Stecker et al., 2005), consistent with the observation that the peak ITDs of rate-ITD curves often fall outside the physiologically plausible range (McAlpine and Grothe, 2003; Grothe et al., 2010; but see also Joris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The peak ITDs of rate-ITD curves often fall outside the physiologically plausible range.
source: Rate-based models generally predict that neuronal responses carry most information at the steepest slopes of neural-discharge-rate versus ITD curves, where neural discharge changes most strongly (Stecker et al., 2005), consistent with the observation that the peak ITDs of rate-ITD curves often fall outside the physiologically plausible range (McAlpine and Grothe, 2003; Grothe et al., 2010; but see also Joris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies, though with a noted exception.

claim: How mammalian sound localization adapts to stimulus history supports a rate-based neural population code.
source: In addition, some authors have suggested that how mammalian sound localization adapts to stimulus history further supports a rate-based neural population code, as assessed behaviorally or via magnetoencephalography (Phillips and Hall, 2005; Stange et al., 2013; Salminen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: It is unknown which of the two competing models (labelled-line versus rate-code model) describes human sound localization better.
source: It is unknown which of the two competing models, broadly characterized as labelled-line versus rate-code model, describes human sound localization better.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The two different models (labelled-line versus rate-code) predict different dependencies of sound localization on sound intensity.
source: Here, we observe that the two different models predict different dependencies of sound localization on sound intensity.
evidence: This is an observation derived from theoretical analysis of the models.

claim: Birds and mammals use different neural mechanisms to calculate sound direction.
source: An extensive physiology literature characterizes labelled-line versus population-rate type neurons and suggests that, at least from the perspective of evolution, birds and mammals use different neural mechanisms to calculate sound direction (review: Grothe, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a cited review.

claim: Peña et al. (1996) characterized labelled-line neurons at low sound levels and as a function of both sound level and ITD.
source: Thus, we searched the avian and mammalian physiology literature and identified two studies that characterized labelled-line versus population rate-code neurons at low sound levels and as a function of both sound level and ITD (Peña et al., 1996; Zwiers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Zwiers et al. (2004) characterized population rate-code neurons at low sound levels and as a function of both sound level and ITD.
source: Thus, we searched the avian and mammalian physiology literature and identified two studies that characterized labelled-line versus population rate-code neurons at low sound levels and as a function of both sound level and ITD (Peña et al., 1996; Zwiers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Both Peña et al. (1996) and Zwiers et al. (2004) report neural firing rate in response to acoustic noise stimuli.
source: Both Peña et al. (1996) and Zwiers et al. (2004) report neural firing rate in response to acoustic noise stimuli and are thus suitable for predicting each model's sensitivity to the acoustic noises we tested in the current study.
evidence: This is based on the cited studies.

claim: The labelled-line neurons predicted that as sound intensity decreases, perceived source laterality would converge towards similar means for low versus high sound intensities, with increased response variability at decreasing sound intensities.
source: The labelled-line neurons predicted that, as sound intensity decreases, perceived source laterality would converge towards similar means for low versus high sound intensities, with increased response variability at decreasing sound intensities (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model based on reconstructed neural data, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The hemispheric-difference model predicted that as sound intensity decreases to near threshold levels, perceived laterality would become increasingly biased toward the midline reference.
source: In contrast, the hemispheric-difference model predicted that as sound intensity decreases to near threshold levels, perceived laterality would become increasingly biased toward the midline reference (Figure 1D, for example note the shallower slope and thus compressed laterality percepts for red versus blue curves).
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model based on reconstructed neural data, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: At higher overall sound intensities, both models predicted that lateralization would be intensity invariant.
source: At higher overall sound intensities, both models predicted that lateralization would be intensity invariant (see insets in Figure 1C versus D).
evidence: This is a prediction from both computational models, illustrated in the figure insets.

claim: A listener's ability to discriminate ITD can vary with sound intensity.
source: A listener's ability to discriminate ITD can vary with sound intensity (Dietz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Some studies reported decreased perceived source laterality near sensation threshold.
source: Some reported decreased perceived source laterality near sensation threshold (Teas, 1962; Sabin et al., 2005), but others reported weak or no level effects on perceived lateralization (Von Békésy and Wever, 1960; Mickunas, 1963; Hartmann and Rakerd, 1993; Macpherson and Middlebrooks, 2000; Inoue, 2001; Vliegen and Van Opstal, 2004; Brungart and Simpson, 2008; Gai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Some studies reported weak or no level effects on perceived lateralization.
source: Some reported decreased perceived source laterality near sensation threshold (Teas, 1962; Sabin et al., 2005), but others reported weak or no level effects on perceived lateralization (Von Békésy and Wever, 1960; Mickunas, 1963; Hartmann and Rakerd, 1993; Macpherson and Middlebrooks, 2000; Inoue, 2001; Vliegen and Van Opstal, 2004; Brungart and Simpson, 2008; Gai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: For stimuli at higher sensation levels where the rate-level functions saturate, both the labelled-line and the hemispheric difference model predict level invariance.
source: For instance, assuming an approximately 30 dB dynamic range of rate-level function either at the MSO or downstream in the binaural pathway (e.g. medial superior olive: Goldberg and Brown, 1968; inferior colliculus: Zwiers et al., 2004), for stimuli at higher sensation levels (SL) where the rate-level functions saturate, both the labelled-line and the hemispheric difference model predict level invariance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of neural rate-level functions and cited studies.

claim: For low-frequency sound, listeners rely dominantly on ITD when judging lateral source angle.
source: For low-frequency sound, listeners rely dominantly on ITD when judging lateral source angle.
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory perception.

claim: For broadband sound, listeners integrate across all three types of spatial cue (ITD, interaural level differences, and spectral cues).
source: However, for broadband sound, listeners integrate across all three types of spatial cue (Wightman and Kistler, 1992; Ihlefeld and Shinn-Cunningham, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Unlike ITDs, interaural level differences and overall sound intensity both decrease with increasing source distance.
source: Unlike ITDs, interaural level differences and overall sound intensity both decrease with increasing source distance, raising the possibility that for stimuli with high-frequency content, listeners judged softer sounds to be more medial because they interpreted them to be farther away than louder sounds.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of acoustic physics and perception.

claim: The literature provides insufficient evidence on how ITD-based lateralization varies with sound level near sensation threshold.
source: Thus, the literature provides insufficient evidence on how ITD-based lateralization varies with sound level near sensation threshold.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The labelled-line code hypothesis predicted that the mean perceived direction based on ITD would be intensity invariant, even at intensities close to sensation level.
source: The labelled-line code hypothesis predicted that the mean perceived direction based on ITD would be intensity invariant, even at intensities close to SL.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the labelled-line model.

claim: Stimuli consisted of low-frequency noise tokens that were bandlimited to cover most of the frequency range where humans can discriminate ITD (corner frequencies from 300 to 1200 Hz).
source: Stimuli consisted of low-frequency noise tokens that were bandlimited to cover most of the frequency range where humans can discriminate ITD (Brughera et al., 2013; here, corner frequencies from 300 to 1200 Hz, shown in Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli used in the study, with reference to a cited study and a figure.

claim: The NLME model predicts 80.6% of the variance in the measured responses for spectrally flat noise.
source: This model predicts 80.6% of the variance in the measured responses and is deemed an appropriate fit of the data.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Perceived laterality scores increased with increasing ITD.
source: Perceived laterality scores increased with increasing ITD, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data.

claim: With decreasing sound intensity, percepts were increasingly biased towards midline.
source: With decreasing sound intensity, percepts were increasingly biased towards midline (compare order of colored lines, magnified in the inset of Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The NLME model for inverse A-weighted noise accounts for 80.4% of the variance in the data.
source: This second model accounts for 80.4% of the variance in the data, closely fitting the measured responses.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The results confirm the effect of biasing perceived laterality toward midline with decreasing sound intensity for both spectrally flat noise and A-weighted noise.
source: Thus, the results confirm the effect of biasing perceived laterality toward midline with decreasing sound intensity. Therefore, for both spectrally flat noise and A-weighted noise, statistical analyses, which partialed out overall differences between listeners, are inconsistent with a labelled-line model of human sound localization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Statistical analyses are inconsistent with a labelled-line model of human sound localization.
source: Thus, the results confirm the effect of biasing perceived laterality toward midline with decreasing sound intensity. Therefore, for both spectrally flat noise and A-weighted noise, statistical analyses, which partialed out overall differences between listeners, are inconsistent with a labelled-line model of human sound localization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Visual depth is computed in the cerebral cortex based on signals from the two eyes.
source: In analogy to sound localization based on the comparison of signals from the two ears (Figure 3A), visual depth is computed in the cerebral cortex based on signals from the two eyes (Figure 3B; Poggio, 1995; Parker and Cumming, 2001; Parker, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies and illustrated in a figure.

claim: In both primary V1 and extrastriate V3a cortex of rhesus macaque monkeys, three types of neurons are thought to encode binocular disparity.
source: Specifically, in both primary V1 and extrastriate V3a cortex of rhesus macaque monkeys, three types of neurons are thought to encode binocular disparity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in visual neuroscience.

claim: Tuned-excitatory neurons respond best to zero spatial disparity between the two eyes.
source: 'Tuned-excitatory' neurons respond best to zero spatial disparity between the two eyes, whereas 'near cells' respond more vigorously when an object approaches, increasing crossed disparity between the eyes (Parker and Cumming, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Near cells respond more vigorously when an object approaches, increasing crossed disparity between the eyes.
source: 'Tuned-excitatory' neurons respond best to zero spatial disparity between the two eyes, whereas 'near cells' respond more vigorously when an object approaches, increasing crossed disparity between the eyes (Parker and Cumming, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Far cells fire more vigorously as uncrossed disparity increases.
source: Finally, 'far cells' fire more vigorously as uncrossed disparity increases.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in visual neuroscience.

claim: In V1, the most frequently encountered type of binocular neurons are of the tuned-excitatory type.
source: In V1, the most frequently encountered type of binocular neurons are of the tuned-excitatory type.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in visual neuroscience.

claim: In V3a the large majority of neurons is stereo-specific and most neurons are either near or far cells.
source: However, in V3a the large majority of neurons is stereo-specific (Poggio et al., 1988) and most neurons are either near or far cells.
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Unlike V1 activity, the activity in cortical area V3a predicts behavioral performance on tasks involving stereoscopic depth.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging experiments on human stereoscopic vision found that unlike V1 activity, the activity in cortical area V3a predicts behavioral performance on tasks involving stereoscopic depth (Backus et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: The central nervous system has evolved a canonical computation that is common to different sensory modalities for computing perceptual space from sensory input.
source: These observations lead us to propose that in order to compute perceptual space from sensory input, the central nervous system has evolved a canonical computation that is common to different sensory modalities.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the analogies between auditory and visual findings.

claim: Near and far cells encode visual distance from the fixation plane in a way similar to how inferior colliculus neurons encode auditory azimuthal angle away from midline reference.
source: Specifically, we propose that near and far cells encode visual distance from the fixation plane in a way similar to how inferior colliculus neurons encode auditory azimuthal angle away from midline reference: firing rate increases monotonically with distance from perceptual reference anchor or fixation.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the analogies between auditory and visual findings.

claim: In both the auditory and the visual system, the same cells that are tuned to binaural ITD or binocular disparity also have intensity-response functions.
source: We observe that in both the auditory and the visual system, the same cells that are tuned to binaural ITD or binocular disparity also have intensity-response functions.
evidence: This is an observation based on established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: A rate-code based on a population of cells tuned to binaural ITD or binocular disparity should cause ambiguities when stimulated below the saturation firing rate, either at low sound intensity or at low contrast.
source: A rate-code based on a population of these cells should cause ambiguities when stimulated below the saturation firing rate, either at low sound intensity or at low contrast (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of rate-coding and illustrated in a figure.

claim: One study found that low visual contrast affects the computation of depth, but only in some observers.
source: Indeed, one study found such an effect, but only in some observers (Cisarik and Harwerth, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Several studies on depth perception indicate that low contrast is interpreted by the brain as a cue for distance; lower contrast targets are perceived farther away.
source: Several studies on depth perception indicate that low contrast is interpreted by the brain as a cue for distance; lower contrast targets are perceived farther away (e.g. Schor and Howarth, 1986; Rohaly and Wilson, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Experiments that controlled for low contrast bias demonstrated that low contrast causes perceived depth to shrink, both for near and far deviations from baseline.
source: However, experiments that controlled for low contrast bias demonstrated that low contrast causes perceived depth to shrink, both for near and far deviations from baseline (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: There is a link between population rate-coding and stimulus intensity in perceived visual depth as in perceived auditory azimuth.
source: Thus, there is a link between population rate-coding and stimulus intensity in perceived visual depth as in perceived auditory azimuth, two perceptual spatial dimensions computed by the brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of auditory and visual findings.

claim: Most rate-code models rely on subtractive comparisons between populations of neurons that are tuned to opposite hemifields, inherently sharing ambiguous readouts at low suprathreshold sound intensities.
source: Most of these rate-code models rely on subtractive comparisons between populations of neurons that are tuned to opposite hemifields, inherently sharing ambiguous readouts at low suprathreshold sound intensities.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of rate-code models in the literature.

claim: Divisive comparisons between ipsi- and contralaterally tuned neural populations are less likely to predict the observed behavioral bias due to stimulus intensity.
source: In contrast, divisive comparisons between ipsi- and contralaterally tuned neural populations are less likely to predict the observed behavioral bias due to stimulus intensity (Groh, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: It has been suggested that depending on perceptual task, the mammalian brain could combine place- and rate-codes.
source: Moreover, it has been suggested that depending on perceptual task, the mammalian brain could combine place- and rate-codes (Porter and Groh, 2006; Goodman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The mammalian auditory pathway may convert place- into rate-codes and vice versa.
source: For instance, the mammalian auditory pathway may convert place- into rate-codes and vice versa (Groh et al., 2003; Porter and Groh, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Downstream from the inferior colliculus, rate-coding seems to be maintained, at least in the superior colliculus of rhesus macaque.
source: However, downstream from the inferior colliculus, rate-coding seems to be maintained, at least in the superior colliculus of rhesus macaque (Werner-Reiss and Groh, 2008; Lee and Groh, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Psychophysical and computational results suggest that for sound localization based on ITD at low sound levels, cortical maps do not play a role.
source: Moreover, our psychophysical and computational results suggest that for sound localization based on ITD at low sound levels, cortical maps do not play a role.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's results.

claim: There is good evidence for spatial map-like signals in higher order auditory cortical fields when interaural level differences are present, at medium to high sound levels.
source: However, there is good evidence for spatial map-like signals in higher order auditory cortical fields when interaural level differences are present, at medium to high sound levels (Higgins et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Excitatory-excitatory (EE) cells in auditory cortex that are tuned to sound locations near midline are also often tuned for sound intensity.
source: For instance, excitatory-excitatory (EE) cells in auditory cortex that are tuned to sound locations near midline are also often tuned for sound intensity (Semple and Kitzes, 1993; Pollak et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2004; Razak and Fuzessery, 2010; Higgins et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Unlike predictions from a rate-code neuronal readout, labelled-line coding predicts that sound localization is intensity invariant.
source: In summary, unlike predictions from a rate-code neuronal readout, labelled-line coding predicts that sound localization is intensity invariant.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the labelled-line model.

claim: For low frequency noise, where ITDs are the dominant localization cue, and at low sound intensities, sound lateralization based on ITD is not intensity invariant; it becomes increasingly medially biased with decreasing sensation level.
source: Our experimental results show that for low frequency noise, where ITDs are the dominant localization cue, and at low sound intensities, sound lateralization based on ITD is not intensity invariant; it becomes increasingly medially biased with decreasing SL.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data.

claim: The observed localization bias is overall small in magnitude, showing that the brain can robustly localize based on ITD across a large range of sound intensities.
source: The observed localization bias is overall small in magnitude, showing that the brain can robustly localize based on ITD across a large range of sound intensities.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The localization bias is of theoretical importance as it confirms the prediction of a subtractive rate-based neuronal readout.
source: However, this bias is of theoretical importance as it confirms the prediction of a subtractive rate-based neuronal readout.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing experimental results with model predictions.

claim: The auditory finding parallels a phenomenon of visual fixation bias when calculating visual distance from binocular disparity at low contrast.
source: Moreover, our auditory finding parallels a phenomenon of visual fixation bias when calculating visual distance from binocular disparity at low contrast.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing auditory and visual findings.

claim: The perceptual data on auditory localization together with previously published data on visual distance perception are parsimonious with the idea that a population rate-code underlies the brain's computation of location.
source: Instead, our perceptual data on auditory localization together with previously published data on visual distance perception are parsimonious with the idea that a population rate-code underlies the brain's computation of location.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's results and comparison with visual literature.

claim: Twelve naïve normal-hearing listeners (ages 18–27, five females) were enrolled in this study.
source: Twelve naïve normal-hearing listeners (ages 18–27, five females) were enrolled in this study and paid for their time.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Listeners' audiometric thresholds were 25 dB hearing level or better at octave frequencies from 250 to 8000 Hz.
source: Their audiometric thresholds, as assessed via a calibrated GSI 39 Auto Tymp device (Grason-Stadler), were 25 dB hearing level or better at octave frequencies from 250 to 8000 Hz, and did not differ by more than 10 dB across ears at each octave frequency.
evidence: This describes the hearing characteristics of the study participants.

claim: Ten listeners reached training criterion, suggesting that they were able to consistently report where they perceived the sounds based on ITD.
source: Ten listeners reached criterion, suggesting that they were able to consistently report where they perceived the sounds based on ITD.
evidence: This is a result from the training phase of the experiment.
